2. The 'animus deserendi' can develop after the initial physical separation.
3. The burden of proof lies heavily on the petitioner to prove both the physical separation and
the intention to desert.

cases.title: Chetan Dass v. Kamla Devi
cases.facts:
Chetan Dass (husband) filed for divorce against Kamla Devi (wife) on the ground of desertion and
cruelty. However, the evidence presented in the lower courts clearly established that the husband
was living in an adulterous relationship with another woman. It was this affair that caused the
matrimonial strife and forced the wife to live separately. In the Supreme Court, the husband argued
that regardless of his affair, the marriage was completely dead and had irretrievably broken down, so
a divorce should be granted to end the suffering.
cases.issues:
1. Can a husband who is actively engaging in an extramarital affair seek a divorce on the
ground that the marriage has irretrievably broken down?
2. How does Section 23(1)(a) of the Hindu Marriage Act restrict the granting of relief to a
wrongdoer?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The husband argued that keeping a dead marriage alive on paper serves no purpose. He admitted
his affair but argued that the wife's refusal to grant a divorce out of spite was cruelty in itself.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The wife argued that the husband destroyed the marriage through his adultery. She was willing to live
with him if he left the other woman. Granting him a divorce would mean rewarding his infidelity.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court dismissed the husband's divorce petition, strictly applying the doctrine
that a person cannot take advantage of their own wrong.
cases.reasoning:
The Court heavily relied on Section 23(1)(a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, which states that a court shall
grant relief only if it is satisfied that the petitioner is not taking advantage of his or her own wrong. The
Court held that the husband's brazen adulterous relationship was the root cause of the separation.
The wife was perfectly justified in living separately. The Court rebuked the husband's attempt to use
the concept of 'irretrievable breakdown'. The Court ruled that 'irretrievable breakdown' cannot be
used as a backdoor by an offending spouse to escape a marriage they deliberately destroyed.
Granting a divorce would legally validate his adultery and allow him to profit from his own tortious
conduct against his wife.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A spouse cannot seek equitable or statutory relief (divorce) if they are the primary wrongdoer
responsible for the marital breakdown.
2. Irretrievable breakdown of marriage cannot be pleaded by a spouse whose blatant adultery
caused the breakdown.
3. Section 23(1)(a) serves as an absolute bar against rewarding matrimonial misconduct.

cases.title: Darshan Gupta v. Radhika Gupta
cases.facts:
The husband filed for divorce on the ground of mental cruelty, alleging that the wife had filed false
criminal complaints and behaved erratically. The trial court and the High Court found that the
husband's allegations were entirely baseless. In fact, it was the husband who had subjected the wife
to immense cruelty, demanding dowry and eventually throwing her out. Despite the husband's cruelty,
the wife maintained throughout the litigation that she was ready and willing to live with him. The
husband appealed to the Supreme Court, requesting the court to invoke Article 142 to grant a divorce
because the marriage was practically dead.
cases.issues:
1. Should the Supreme Court invoke Article 142 to dissolve a marriage on the ground of
irretrievable breakdown if one spouse is completely innocent and desires cohabitation?
2. Can the fault theory be entirely ignored in favor of the breakdown theory?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The husband argued that they had been separated for over 12 years. The litigation was bitter, and
resuming cohabitation was a factual impossibility. He urged the court to dissolve the marriage under
Article 142 to do 'complete justice'.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The wife argued that she was the victim of his dowry demands and cruelty. She had never committed
any marital offense and was still willing to fulfill her marital obligations. Forcing a divorce on her would
be a gross injustice.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court refused to grant the divorce, holding that Article 142 cannot be used to
penalize a blameless spouse.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a critical judgment on the limits of the 'irretrievable breakdown' doctrine. The
Court held that while Article 142 gives the Supreme Court the power to do complete justice, this
power must be exercised equitably. If one spouse is completely at fault (the husband, who demanded
dowry and ousted her) and the other spouse is completely blameless and willing to cohabit, granting
a divorce on the sole ground that 'the marriage is dead' would be a miscarriage of justice. It would
amount to the court assisting the wrongdoer in achieving his objective of getting rid of his innocent
wife. The Court explicitly ruled that irretrievable breakdown cannot be invoked by the erring party
against an innocent party who refuses to consent.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Irretrievable breakdown of marriage is not a statutory ground and cannot be applied
mechanically.
2. Article 142 will not be invoked to dissolve a marriage if the opposing spouse is entirely
blameless and willing to cohabit.
3. The court will not allow an abusive or at-fault spouse to force a divorce on an innocent victim.

cases.title: K.V. Prakash Babu v. State of Karnataka
cases.facts:
The appellant husband was allegedly involved in an extra-marital affair. When the wife discovered the
affair, she was deeply distressed and confronted him. Unable to cope with the betrayal and the
husband's refusal to end the affair, she committed suicide. The husband was charged under Section
498A (cruelty) and Section 306 (abetment to suicide) of the IPC. The prosecution argued that his
blatant infidelity amounted to extreme mental cruelty, which drove her to take her own life.
cases.issues:
1. Does an extra-marital affair, by itself, constitute 'cruelty' under Section 498A of the IPC?
2. Does infidelity amount to 'abetment of suicide' under Section 306 of the IPC?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The State argued that in Indian society, a husband's infidelity causes immense psychological trauma
to the wife. Driving a spouse to such despair that she commits suicide squarely falls within the
definition of mental cruelty and abetment.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The husband argued that while adultery is a moral wrong and a civil ground for divorce, it does not
automatically translate to criminal cruelty or abetment to suicide unless accompanied by active
harassment, physical abuse, or dowry demands.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court acquitted the husband, holding that an extra-marital affair, without more,
does not attract Section 498A or 306 IPC.
cases.reasoning:
The Court drew a strict line between a civil matrimonial offense and a criminal offense. The Court
held that an extra-marital relationship is illegal (as a ground for divorce) and immoral, but to constitute
criminal 'cruelty' under Section 498A, there must be evidence of willful conduct that is of such a
nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide. Mere suspicion or even certainty of an affair
does not fulfill the strict criteria of criminal mens rea for abetment. Unless the husband actively
harassed, physically abused, or taunted the wife to the point where she had no option but to die, he
cannot be convicted under 306 IPC. The wife's extreme emotional reaction to his infidelity, while
tragic, does not make him legally culpable for her suicide.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. An extra-marital affair is a ground for civil divorce but does not inherently constitute criminal
cruelty under Section 498A IPC.
2. Infidelity does not amount to 'abetment of suicide' (Section 306 IPC) without active, persistent
harassment or instigation.
3. Criminal liability requires strict proof of malicious intent and active instigation, not just moral
failings.

cases.title: Raj Talreja v. Kavita Talreja
cases.facts:
The marriage was troubled from the start. The wife made numerous sensational and defamatory
allegations against the husband and his family members. She filed multiple complaints with the
police, the Chief Minister, and other authorities, accusing the husband of extreme physical assault,
attempted murder, and severe dowry harassment. Based on her complaints, the husband and his
elderly parents were arrested and had to spend time in jail before being acquitted, as the courts
found the allegations to be entirely fabricated. The husband filed for divorce on the ground of mental
cruelty.
cases.issues:
1. Does the filing of false, unsubstantiated police complaints leading to the arrest of a spouse
constitute mental cruelty?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The husband argued that the wife's calculated campaign to destroy his reputation, put him behind
bars, and harass his elderly parents through the criminal justice system caused him unimaginable
mental agony, making cohabitation impossible.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The wife argued she was merely exercising her legal rights to seek police intervention for what she
perceived as wrongs, and this should not be weaponized against her in a divorce proceeding.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court granted a decree of divorce to the husband on the ground of extreme
mental cruelty.
cases.reasoning:
The Court categorically held that making reckless, defamatory, and false accusations against a
spouse and his family members constitutes severe mental cruelty. The Court noted that the wife's
actions went far beyond normal matrimonial disputes. By filing fabricated criminal charges that
resulted in the actual arrest and incarceration of the husband and his parents, she inflicted grave
public humiliation and psychological trauma. The Court stated that no person can be expected to live
under the constant fear of being thrown into jail on fake charges by their spouse. When a spouse
misuses the legal machinery to harass the other, it unequivocally destroys the foundation of trust in
the marriage, justifying a divorce.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Filing false criminal complaints that lead to the arrest or harassment of a spouse is a clear act
of mental cruelty.
2. Malicious prosecution destroys the marital bond and provides a valid statutory ground for
divorce under the HMA.
3. The 'wear and tear' defense cannot shield a spouse who weaponizes the police against their
partner.

cases.title: Vishwanath Agrawal v. Sarla Vishwanath Agrawal
cases.facts:
A bitter matrimonial dispute led the wife to launch a public campaign against her husband, a
respected businessman. She gave interviews to local newspapers and published articles wherein she
explicitly described her husband as a 'womanizer', a 'drunkard', and a person of loose morals who
consorted with prostitutes. These articles were widely read in their community. The husband filed for
divorce, claiming that this public character assassination caused him intense humiliation, loss of
reputation, and severe mental cruelty.
cases.issues:
1. Can public defamation and character assassination by a spouse in print media constitute
mental cruelty under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The husband argued that reputation is an integral part of a person's dignity. The wife's deliberate act
of publishing scandalous allegations in the newspaper destroyed his social standing and caused
deep psychological suffering.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The wife argued that her statements were an outburst of a frustrated woman and should be seen in
the context of their marital strife, rather than as a calculated act of cruelty.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court granted the divorce, ruling that public defamation by a spouse is a
severe form of mental cruelty.
cases.reasoning:
The Court emphasized that in Indian society, social reputation and respect are highly valued. When a
wife goes to the press and publishes highly scandalous and defamatory material about her husband,
calling him a womanizer and a drunkard, it inflicts an irreparable blow to his public image and self-
esteem. The Court noted that such conduct is not a private quarrel behind closed doors; it is a public
spectacle that permanently damages the husband's standing in society. This deliberate character
assassination causes profound mental agony and constitutes mental cruelty of the highest order,
making it impossible for the husband to live with her.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Publishing defamatory and scandalous allegations against a spouse in the media constitutes
extreme mental cruelty.
2. The destruction of a spouse's social reputation goes beyond normal matrimonial friction and
justifies a divorce.
3. Character assassination is a violation of the spouse's right to live with dignity.

cases.title: U. Suvetha v. State By Inspector of Police
cases.facts:
A wife filed an FIR under Section 498A of the IPC against her husband and his alleged paramour
(girlfriend), Suvetha. The wife alleged that her husband and Suvetha jointly harassed her and
subjected her to cruelty. Suvetha approached the court to quash the proceedings against her, arguing
that Section 498A applies only to the 'husband or the relative of the husband'. Since she was merely
a girlfriend and not legally related to the husband by blood or marriage, she could not be prosecuted
under this specific section.
cases.issues:
1. What is the definition of a 'relative of the husband' under Section 498A of the IPC?
2. Can a husband's girlfriend, concubine, or paramour be prosecuted for cruelty under
Section 498A?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Suvetha argued that penal statutes must be strictly construed. Since she had no legal tie of blood,
marriage, or adoption to the husband, she did not fall under the statutory category of a 'relative'.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The State and the wife argued that Suvetha was living with the husband and actively participating in
the harassment. Allowing her to escape liability based on a technical definition of 'relative' would
defeat the purpose of the anti-cruelty law.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court quashed the 498A proceedings against the girlfriend, strictly interpreting
the term 'relative'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the rule of strict interpretation for penal statutes. It held that the word 'relative' is
not defined in the IPC, so it must be understood in its ordinary legal sense. A 'relative' means a
person connected by blood, marriage, or adoption. A girlfriend, paramour, or concubine has no legal
recognition as a relative. Therefore, even if the girlfriend actively harassed the wife, she cannot be
charged under Section 498A, which is a special provision targeted exclusively at the husband and his
legal family. (However, the Court noted she could potentially be charged under general penal
provisions for assault or criminal intimidation, but not 498A).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A 'relative' under Section 498A IPC must be connected to the husband by blood, marriage, or
adoption.
2. A girlfriend, paramour, or concubine does not fall within the ambit of 'relative' and cannot be
prosecuted under 498A.
3. Strict interpretation of penal statutes prevents the expansion of criminal liability beyond
legislative intent.

cases.title: Yashita Sahu v. State of Rajasthan
cases.facts:
An Indian couple was living in the USA and had a daughter born there (a US citizen). Marital disputes
arose, and the US court passed an order granting joint custody and injuncting the wife from taking
the child out of the jurisdiction. In direct violation of the US court's order, the wife secretly fled to India
with the child. The husband filed a petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus in the Rajasthan High Court,
seeking the immediate repatriation of the child to the USA. The wife argued that the child was safe
with her in India and that Indian courts should decide the custody based on welfare, ignoring the US
order.
cases.issues:
1. When a child is removed from a foreign jurisdiction in violation of a court order, should
Indian courts issue a writ of habeas corpus to repatriate the child?
2. How do courts balance the 'comity of courts' with the 'welfare of the child'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The father argued that the wife's act was parental child abduction. He relied on the principle of
'comity of courts', arguing that Indian courts should respect the US court's pre-existing jurisdiction
and order the child's return so the US court could adjudicate the matter.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The mother argued that a writ of habeas corpus does not apply because a mother's custody is not
'illegal detention'. She argued that moving the child back to the US would disrupt her life and welfare.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court directed the mother to return to the USA with the child, enforcing the
principle of comity while safeguarding the child's welfare.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reiterated that in all child custody matters, the welfare of the child is the paramount
consideration, overriding even the principle of comity of courts. However, welfare is often best served
by allowing the court with the most intimate contact with the child (the US court, where the child was
born and lived) to decide the matter. The Court held that the mother's unilateral, illegal removal of the
child should not be rewarded. The Court issued a writ of habeas corpus directing the return of the
child to the US jurisdiction. To protect the mother and child, the Court ordered the father to arrange
for their safe travel, accommodation, and legal expenses in the US, ensuring a fair trial there.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. In transnational parental abduction cases, Indian courts respect the 'comity of courts' if it
aligns with the child's welfare.
2. A writ of habeas corpus is maintainable if a child is illegally removed from the jurisdiction of a
competent foreign court.
3. The court of the country where the child has the most intimate contact and established roots
is generally best suited to decide custody.

cases.title: Vivek Singh v. Romani Singh
cases.facts:
A bitter custody battle over an 8-year-old girl. The father had forcibly kept the child away from the
mother for several years. During this period, he systematically poisoned the child's mind against the
mother, telling her the mother did not love her. When the court interviewed the child, she expressed a
strong desire to stay with the father and intense hatred for the mother. The father used the child's
preference as his primary argument for retaining custody.
cases.issues:
1. Should a court follow the stated preference of a child if that preference is the result of
psychological manipulation by one parent?
2. How should Indian courts address 'Parental Alienation Syndrome' (PAS) in custody
disputes?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The mother argued that the child's hostility was unnatural and the direct result of the father's
malicious brainwashing. She argued that leaving the child with the abuser would permanently destroy
the child's psychological health.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The father relied on Section 17(3) of the Guardian and Wards Act, which requires the court to
consider the preference of the child if they are old enough to form an intelligent preference.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court recognized 'Parental Alienation Syndrome' and granted full custody to
the mother, overriding the child's stated preference.
cases.reasoning:
The Court explicitly recognized 'Parental Alienation Syndrome' (PAS) in Indian jurisprudence. PAS
occurs when one parent uses psychological manipulation to turn the child against the other parent,
resulting in the child's unwarranted rejection of the alienated parent. The Court noted that the father's
conduct of alienating the child from the mother was a severe form of psychological abuse. While a
child's preference is important, a court cannot blindly follow it if the child's mind has been tutored or
poisoned. To cure the PAS and ensure the child's holistic psychological welfare, the Court ruled that
the child must be removed from the toxic environment of the alienator (the father) and placed in the
custody of the mother, allowing their bond to heal over time.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Judicial recognition of Parental Alienation Syndrome (PAS) as a form of psychological abuse.
2. A child's preference is not binding on the court if it is the result of tutoring or brainwashing by
one parent.
3. The welfare of the child may necessitate transferring custody to the alienated parent to repair
the psychological damage.

cases.title: Tejaswini Gaud v. Shekhar Jagdish Prasad Tewari
cases.facts:
The mother of an infant child fell terminally ill shortly after childbirth. During her illness and
subsequent death, the child was cared for by the mother's sister (the aunt). After the mother's death,
the biological father sought custody of his child. The aunt refused to hand over the child, arguing that
she had raised the child since birth, the child was deeply attached to her, and uprooting the child
would cause trauma. The father filed a writ of habeas corpus to gain custody.
cases.issues:
1. Who has the primary right to custody of a minor child after the mother's death: the
biological father or the extended relatives who cared for the child?
2. Can a writ of habeas corpus be used by a natural guardian to recover custody from
relatives?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The father argued that under Section 6 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, he is the sole
surviving natural guardian. He argued that unless he is proven completely unfit, no relative has the
right to deny him custody of his own flesh and blood. The aunt's retention of the child was illegal
detention.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The aunt argued that the 'welfare of the child' is paramount, not the statutory right of the father. Since
the child knew only the aunt as a mother figure, shifting custody would be detrimental to the child's
welfare.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court granted custody to the biological father, enforcing his rights as the
natural guardian.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reiterated that while the welfare of the child is paramount, there is a strong legal and
natural presumption that the welfare of the child lies with the biological parent. Extended relatives
(like an aunt or grandparents) cannot retain custody against the wishes of a biological father unless
they can conclusively prove that the father is entirely unfit or that living with him would be harmful.
Mere attachment or the fact that the aunt took care of the child during a crisis does not extinguish the
father's paramount right to raise his child. The Court held that the aunt's refusal to hand over the child
amounted to illegal detention, making the writ of habeas corpus perfectly maintainable.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The biological father has a paramount right to custody after the mother's death, superior to all
extended relatives.
2. Relatives cannot claim custody based merely on attachment or past caretaking unless the
biological parent is proven unfit.
3. A writ of habeas corpus is maintainable by a natural guardian against relatives illegally
withholding the child.

cases.title: Gaytri Bajaj v. Jiten Bhalla
cases.facts:
Following a highly acrimonious divorce, the father obtained custody of their two daughters. The
mother was granted visitation rights. However, the father systematically alienated the children from
the mother. Over time, the children began to vehemently refuse to meet the mother, creating scenes
in court and outright rejecting any contact with her. The father argued that the court should respect
the children's wishes and terminate the mother's visitation rights entirely, claiming that forcing them to
meet her was causing them trauma.
cases.issues:
1. Should a court terminate a mother's visitation rights completely if the children express a
strong, unyielding reluctance to meet her?
2. Is continuous contact with both parents essential for a child's psychological welfare?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The mother argued that the children's hostility was manufactured by the father. She pleaded that
severing all ties would destroy any chance of ever rebuilding her relationship with her daughters.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The father argued that the court's role is to protect the children's welfare, which, in this case, meant
respecting their trauma and not forcing them into unwanted meetings.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court refused to permanently terminate the mother's visitation rights,
emphasizing the necessity of parental contact.
cases.reasoning:
The Court acknowledged the difficult situation where children have been heavily influenced to hate
one parent. However, the Court ruled that the welfare of a child is not determined solely by the child's
current, possibly manipulated, desires. For the holistic psychological development of a child, contact
with both the mother and the father is absolutely essential. Completely cutting off the mother would
be detrimental to the children's long-term emotional health and would reward the father's alienating
behavior. Even if the meetings are initially difficult or resisted, the court must facilitate contact. The
Court ordered supervised visitations and psychological counseling to help rebuild the broken
maternal bond.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A child's reluctance or refusal to meet a parent is not a sufficient ground to permanently
terminate visitation rights.
2. Contact with both parents is a fundamental component of a child's holistic welfare and
psychological development.
3. Courts must actively facilitate contact and counseling rather than severing ties due to parental
alienation.

cases.title: Chaturbhuj v. Sita Bai
cases.facts:
A husband challenged a maintenance order passed under Section 125 of the CrPC in favor of his
wife. He presented evidence showing that the wife was living in their ancestral home, earning some
income from farming, and receiving financial help from her parents. He argued that because she was
not starving or completely destitute, she was not 'unable to maintain herself' as strictly required by
Section 125, and therefore he had no liability to pay her maintenance.
cases.issues:
1. What is the legal interpretation of the phrase 'unable to maintain herself' in Section 125 of
the CrPC?
2. Does a wife need to be absolutely destitute or living on the streets to claim maintenance?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The husband argued for a strict, literal interpretation. If the wife has any source of income or support
that keeps her alive, she does not qualify for maintenance under the anti-vagrancy provisions of the
CrPC.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The wife argued that her meager agricultural income was insufficient to sustain her. She argued that
a husband cannot escape his liability by forcing his wife to depend on her aging parents.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court dismissed the husband's appeal, ruling that the wife's meager income
did not disqualify her from claiming maintenance.
cases.reasoning:
The Court provided a landmark interpretation of 'unable to maintain herself'. The Court held that this
phrase does not mean the wife must be reduced to absolute destitution, begging, or living on the
streets before she can invoke Section 125. 'Unable to maintain herself' means that the wife is unable
to maintain herself in the same standard of living and comfort that she was accustomed to in her
matrimonial home. Earning a paltry sum or surviving on the charity of her parents does not absolve
the husband of his statutory duty. The court must assess whether her independent income is
sufficient to maintain a dignified lifestyle matching the husband's status. Since her income was clearly
insufficient for this, she was entitled to maintenance.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. 'Unable to maintain herself' does not require proof of absolute destitution or starvation.
2. The wife is entitled to a standard of living consistent with what she enjoyed in the matrimonial
home.
3. Meager independent earnings or charity from parents do not extinguish the husband's
maintenance obligation.

cases.title: Bhuwan Mohan Singh v. Meena
cases.facts:
The wife filed an application for maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC. Due to the husband's
delaying tactics, frequent adjournments, and systemic judicial backlogs, the Family Court took nine
years to finally decide the application and award maintenance. Furthermore, the Family Court
ordered the maintenance to be paid from the date of the order, not the date of the application. The
wife appealed, arguing that she had suffered for nine years without support.
cases.issues:
1. Should maintenance under Section 125 CrPC be awarded from the date of the application
or the date of the order?
2. What is the impact of systemic judicial delay on the rights of a destitute wife?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The wife argued that granting maintenance from the date of the order rewarded the husband for
delaying the trial. She had been deprived of financial support for a decade, defeating the very
purpose of the legislation.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The husband relied on the discretion of the Magistrate, arguing that the normal rule is from the date
of the order, and backdating it 9 years would place an impossible financial burden on him.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled heavily in favor of the wife, directing that maintenance must be
paid from the date of the application.
cases.reasoning:
The Court heavily criticized the Family Courts for allowing maintenance proceedings to drag on for
years. Section 125 is a summary proceeding designed to provide immediate relief to prevent
vagrancy. A delay of nine years makes a mockery of justice. The Court held that while the Magistrate
has discretion, the general rule should be to award maintenance from the date of the application. If a
wife is driven to the court for survival, she needs the money from that very day. Granting it from the
date of the order ignores the starvation and struggles she endured during the pendency of the
litigation and encourages husbands to delay proceedings. The Court mandated that Family Courts
must prioritize and expeditiously dispose of maintenance cases.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Maintenance should ordinarily be awarded from the date of the application, not the date of the
order.
2. Delaying maintenance proceedings defeats the social justice objective of Section 125 CrPC.
3. Husbands cannot be allowed to benefit financially by artificially prolonging litigation.

cases.title: Lalita Toppo v. State of Jharkhand
cases.facts:
Lalita Toppo lived in a long-term live-in relationship with a man, knowing he was already married.
They had a child together. When the man abandoned her, she filed for maintenance under the
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (DV Act). The lower courts rejected her
claim, citing earlier Supreme Court precedents (like Indra Sarma) which held that a live-in
relationship with a married man is not a 'relationship in the nature of marriage', and thus she was not
a 'wife' entitled to maintenance under Section 125 CrPC or the DV Act.
cases.issues:
1. Can a woman in a live-in relationship seek maintenance under the Domestic Violence Act
even if she does not strictly qualify as a 'wife' under Section 125 of the CrPC?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The appellant argued that the DV Act provides a broader definition of 'domestic relationship' than the
strict marital requirements of Section 125 CrPC. She sought relief from economic abuse under the
DV Act, distinct from standard maintenance.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The respondent argued that since the relationship was adulterous, recognizing it for maintenance
under any statute would violate public policy and bypass the restrictions of Section 125 CrPC.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A three-judge bench of the Supreme Court recognized the right of a live-in partner to seek
relief under the DV Act, distinguishing it from Section 125 CrPC.
cases.reasoning:
The Court noted that the Domestic Violence Act, 2005, provides a much broader spectrum of
remedies than Section 125 CrPC. While Section 125 CrPC is strictly limited to a legally wedded 'wife'
(and some specific exceptions), the DV Act is designed to protect 'any woman' who is or has been in
a 'domestic relationship'. The definition of economic abuse under the DV Act includes the deprivation
of financial resources to which the aggrieved woman is entitled. The Court held that even if a woman
does not meet the strict legal criteria of a 'wife' to claim maintenance under the CrPC, she can still
seek monetary relief and protection from economic abuse under the broader, more protective
provisions of the DV Act. This opened a critical alternate legal avenue for women in informal
relationships.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The Domestic Violence Act provides broader financial remedies than Section 125 of the
CrPC.
2. A woman in a live-in relationship can claim monetary relief for economic abuse under the DV
Act, even if she is not a legally wedded wife.
3. The DV Act acts as an independent, more expansive social welfare legislation.

cases.title: Juveria Abdul Majid Patni v. Atif Iqbal Mansoori
cases.facts:
The wife was subjected to severe domestic violence. She eventually left the matrimonial home and
the husband subsequently pronounced an ex-parte 'talaq' (divorce) to sever the marriage. Sometime
after the divorce was pronounced, the wife filed a petition under the Domestic Violence Act seeking
maintenance, residence, and compensation for the abuse she suffered during the marriage. The
husband filed to quash the petition, arguing that since they were divorced at the time she filed the
petition, there was no existing 'domestic relationship', and thus the DV Act could not apply to him.
cases.issues:
1. Can a divorced woman file a petition under the Domestic Violence Act for acts of violence
committed during the subsistence of the marriage?
2. Does the severing of the marital tie extinguish the right to seek civil remedies for past
abuse under the DV Act?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The wife argued that the DV Act defines an aggrieved person as someone who 'is, or has been, in a
domestic relationship'. The violence occurred when she was his wife. Allowing a husband to escape
liability simply by divorcing his victim would render the Act useless.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The husband argued a strict interpretation: once the marriage is over, the domestic relationship
ceases to exist. Civil reliefs under the DV Act are meant to protect a woman currently living in a
shared household, not to act as a post-divorce penal mechanism.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the wife, holding that a divorced woman is fully entitled
to invoke the DV Act for past domestic violence.
cases.reasoning:
The Court focused on the specific phrasing of the DV Act: 'has been in a domestic relationship'. The
Court reasoned that if a woman was subjected to domestic violence while the marriage was
subsisting, her right to seek statutory remedies crystallizes. The husband cannot unilaterally
extinguish her right to compensation, residence, or maintenance simply by pronouncing a divorce.
The past acts of violence constitute a continuing wrong for which she is entitled to seek relief. Any
other interpretation would encourage abusive husbands to quickly divorce their wives the moment
they fear a DV Act complaint, defeating the entire protective purpose of the legislation.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A divorced woman has the locus standi to file a petition under the Domestic Violence Act.
2. The phrase 'has been in a domestic relationship' allows remedies for violence committed
during the past marriage.
3. A husband's unilateral divorce does not absolve him of liability for prior acts of domestic
violence.

cases.title: Shalu Ojha v. Prashant Rajput
cases.facts:
A bitter dispute arose between a husband and wife. The wife filed a complaint under the DV Act and
obtained an interim order granting her the right to reside in the shared household (which belonged to
the husband's father). Despite the court order, she was forcibly evicted from the house by the
husband and his family. The wife approached the courts seeking restoration of her possession of the
shared household under the DV Act.
cases.issues:
1. Can a court order the restoration of possession of a shared household to an aggrieved
woman who has been forcibly evicted?
2. What are the powers of the Magistrate to enforce residence orders under the DV Act?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The wife argued that the DV Act specifically empowers the Magistrate to pass residence orders
preventing eviction, and if an eviction occurs in violation of the law or court orders, the court must
have the power to restore the status quo.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The husband's family argued that since she was physically out of the house, the court could at best
order the husband to provide alternative accommodation, but could not force the in-laws to take her
back into their property.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court upheld the power of the Magistrate to restore the wife's possession of
the shared household.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act is a comprehensive code
designed to provide effective relief. Section 19 of the Act not only empowers the Magistrate to pass
an order restraining the respondents from dispossessing the aggrieved person, but it implicitly
includes the power to direct the restoration of possession if she has already been illegally evicted. If
courts could not restore possession, abusive families would simply physically throw the woman out
and then offer to pay for a cheap alternative rental, entirely defeating the woman's statutory right to
reside in her matrimonial home. The Court held the Magistrate has the power to use police
assistance to break open locks and restore the woman's rightful possession.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Magistrates have the statutory power under the DV Act to restore possession of the shared
household to an illegally evicted woman.
2. Alternative accommodation is not a compulsory substitute if the woman wishes to enforce her
right to the shared household.
3. Police assistance can be mandated to enforce residence orders and protect the woman's
statutory rights.

cases.title: Manish Goel v. Rohini Goel
cases.facts:
A husband and wife filed a joint petition for divorce by mutual consent under Section 13B of the
Hindu Marriage Act. They had been separated for over a year and had settled all their disputes
regarding alimony. They filed an application before the Family Court to waive the mandatory 6-month
statutory waiting period required between the first and second motions, as they wanted an immediate
divorce. The Family Court refused, citing its lack of statutory power. The couple approached the
Supreme Court directly under Article 142, asking the Court to waive the period.
cases.issues:
1. Can the Supreme Court routinely use its extraordinary powers under Article 142 to waive
the statutory 6-month waiting period for mutual divorce?
2. What are the limitations on the use of Article 142 in overriding express statutory
provisions?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The couple argued that since they both agreed and the marriage was irretrievably broken, waiting six
months was an unnecessary formality causing them mental agony. They urged the SC to use Article
142 to do 'complete justice'.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Since it was a mutual petition, there was no opposing party, but the Court had to consider the legal
integrity of bypassing statutory mandates.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court refused to waive the 6-month period, establishing strict limits on the use
of Article 142.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a crucial judgment on judicial discipline. The Court held that Article 142 is a
residual power to do complete justice, but it cannot be used in a manner that is directly contrary to
express statutory provisions. Section 13B(2) of the HMA clearly mandates a 6-month waiting period.
The Supreme Court cannot routinely issue orders that ignore or nullify the clear intent of the
legislature just because the parties ask for it. The Court noted that while it had waived the period in
some past cases, those were rare, exceptional circumstances involving long-drawn, bitter litigation
where the waiting period would cause severe injustice. It cannot become a routine mechanism for
couples to get quick divorces. (Note: This strict view was later softened in Amardeep Singh v.
Harveen Kaur, which held the period was directory, not mandatory)..
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Article 142 cannot be used to routinely override express, mandatory statutory provisions of
the Hindu Marriage Act.
2. The 6-month waiting period for mutual divorce cannot be waived by the Supreme Court
merely upon the request of the parties.
3. The inherent powers of the SC are meant for exceptional cases of gross injustice, not for
judicial legislation.

cases.title: Suman Singh v. Sanjay Singh
cases.facts:
The husband filed for divorce on the ground of mental cruelty. He presented a list of nine specific
incidents spanning a decade of marriage, alleging that his wife misbehaved with him, occasionally
spoke disrespectfully to his parents, and once refused to make tea for his guests. He argued that
these cumulative incidents caused him mental agony and constituted cruelty. The wife contested the
petition, stating she wanted to live with him and that these were minor arguments typical in any
household.
cases.issues:
1. Do isolated, sporadic incidents of friction, arguments, or disrespectful behavior over a long
marriage constitute 'mental cruelty' for granting a divorce?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The husband argued that the continuous disrespect and refusal to perform household duties properly
caused him mental distress, making it impossible to continue the marriage.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The wife argued that these were trivial domestic squabbles. She asserted that no marriage is
completely free of arguments and that defining such minor incidents as cruelty would make every
marriage vulnerable to divorce.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court dismissed the husband's petition, ruling that the cited incidents did not
amount to legal cruelty.
cases.reasoning:
The Court emphasized the concept of 'ordinary wear and tear' in matrimonial life. A marriage is a
complex relationship involving two different personalities, and occasional friction, outbursts of anger,
or minor arguments are inevitable. The Court held that to constitute 'mental cruelty' under the law, the
conduct must be much more severe than ordinary annoyances or differences of opinion. It must be
sustained, unjustifiable conduct that causes a reasonable apprehension in the mind of the spouse
that it is harmful or injurious to live together. Nine isolated incidents over a span of ten years-like
refusing to make tea or arguing with in-laws-are trivialities. Granting a divorce on such flimsy
grounds would destroy the institution of marriage.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Ordinary wear and tear, minor squabbles, and isolated incidents of friction do not constitute
'mental cruelty'.
2. Cruelty must be severe, sustained, and of a nature that makes cohabitation psychologically
harmful or impossible.
3. Courts must distinguish between the normal frustrations of married life and legally actionable
matrimonial misconduct.

cases.title: Neha Tyagi v. Lieutenant Colonel Deepak Tyagi
cases.facts:
The husband (an Army officer) filed for divorce on the ground of extreme mental cruelty by the wife.
The courts found overwhelming evidence that the wife had subjected him to severe harassment, false
complaints, and abuse, and accordingly granted the husband a decree of divorce. However, the
couple had a minor son. After securing the divorce, the husband stopped paying for the child's
education and upbringing, arguing that since the wife destroyed the marriage through her cruelty and
had custody of the child, he should not be financially burdened.
cases.issues:
1. Does a husband's obligation to maintain his child extinguish if the marriage is dissolved
due to the severe cruelty and fault of the wife?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The husband argued that he was the victim of a toxic marriage. He argued it was unjust to force him
to continuously pay the woman who ruined his life, especially when she insisted on keeping the child.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The wife (on behalf of the child) argued that the marital fault of the mother has absolutely no bearing
on the father's independent statutory and moral duty to maintain his son.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court granted the divorce but strictly ordered the husband to pay
comprehensive maintenance and education costs for the child.
cases.reasoning:
The Court firmly separated the marital relationship from the parental relationship. While the wife was
undoubtedly guilty of severe mental cruelty justifying the divorce, the child was an innocent third
party. The statutory and moral obligation of a father to maintain his child is absolute and exists
entirely independent of the wife's conduct. A father cannot use his ex-wife's cruelty as an excuse to
financially abandon his son. The Court held that despite the dissolution of the marriage due to the
wife's fault, the father must continue to bear the full responsibility for the child's maintenance,
healthcare, and education until the child reaches the age of majority and becomes self-sufficient.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A father's obligation to maintain his child is absolute and independent of the marital conduct
of the mother.
2. A decree of divorce granted due to the wife's cruelty does not extinguish the father's financial
liability towards his children.
3. The child's right to maintenance cannot be penalized or diminished due to the matrimonial
faults of the parents.
